st: Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat and fry the sliced onions, stirring often, until deep golden brown, about 20 minutes. Lift them out onto a plate and spread them to crisp.

In a large bowl, mix the mutton with the yogurt, ginger paste, garlic paste, half of the fried onions, the cumin, chili powder, [[1 tsp]] garam masala, the slit chilies and salt. Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 2 hours.
Stir the saffron into the warm milk and leave it to bloom.

Bring [[8 cups]] of water to a boil with the cinnamon, cardamom, bay leaves and plenty of salt. Add the drained rice and boil for 5 to 6 minutes until about 70 percent cooked (the grains should still snap when bitten). Drain well.
Spread the potatoes in the bottom of a heavy pot, then spoon the marinated mutton and all its juices over them.
Cover the meat with half of the rice. Sprinkle with half of the remaining fried onions, then add the rest of the rice.
Top with the last of the fried onions, [[1 tsp]] garam masala, the saffron milk, the rose water and the ghee, drizzling evenly.
Cover the pot with foil and a tight lid. Cook over high heat for 5 minutes, then reduce to the lowest heat and cook for 60 to 70 minutes, without opening, until the mutton is very tender.
Rest the pot off the heat for 10 minutes. Gently fluff and serve the layers together, making sure each plate gets meat, a piece of potato and rice.
Soak both kinds of mustard seeds in [[0.5 cup]] warm water for 15 minutes.
Drain the seeds and grind them in a blender with 2 green chilies, a little salt and a splash of fresh water to a smooth paste. Use only cool water, since warm water makes the paste bitter.
Pat the fish dry and rub it with [[0.5 tsp]] turmeric and salt. Let it sit for 10 minutes.
Heat [[3 tbsp]] mustard oil in a wide pan until it just begins to smoke, then lower the heat a little. Fry the fish for about 1 minute per side without browning. Lift it out.
In the same pan, add [[0.5 tsp]] turmeric and the mustard paste. Stir for 1 minute, then pour in [[1 cup]] water and bring to a simmer.
Slide the fish back in, add the 2 remaining slit green chilies and salt, and simmer gently for 8 to 10 minutes, spooning sauce over the fish. Do not stir hard, so the steaks stay whole.
Drizzle [[1 tbsp]] raw mustard oil over the top and switch off the heat. Serve hot with plain steamed rice and watch for small bones.
Dry roast the dal in a heavy pot over medium heat for 3 minutes, stirring, until it smells nutty and turns light gold.
Rinse the dal and rice together until the water runs clear, then soak them in water for 15 minutes and drain.
Melt the ghee in a large pot over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds, bay leaves, cinnamon, cardamom and cloves and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the onion and fry for 8 to 10 minutes until golden brown.
Stir in the ginger, turmeric, ground cumin and chili powder and cook for 1 minute.
Add the drained rice and dal and fry, stirring, for 3 minutes so every grain is coated in the spices.
Pour in [[5 cups]] hot water, add salt and the slit chilies, and bring to a boil.
Cover, reduce the heat to low, and cook for 25 minutes, stirring once or twice, until the rice and dal are soft and the mixture is thick and porridge-like.
Rest, covered, for 5 minutes, then stir and serve hot.
Heat the mustard oil in a heavy pot over medium heat until it smells sharp and just starts to smoke, then lower the heat.
Add the cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, bay leaves and dried chilies and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the onions and fry slowly for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring often, until deep brown.
Stir in the ginger paste and garlic paste and fry for 3 minutes. Add the chili powder, coriander, cumin and turmeric with a splash of water so the spices do not burn.
Add the beef and salt. Raise the heat to medium-high and fry, stirring, for 12 to 15 minutes until the beef is browned and the oil begins to separate.
Pour in [[1 cup]] hot water, cover, reduce to low, and cook for 90 minutes. Stir every 15 minutes and add a splash of the remaining hot water if it sticks.
Uncover when the beef is tender. Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly, for 10 minutes until the sauce clings to the meat and turns very dark brown.
Stir in the garam masala, taste for salt, and serve with plain rice or paratha.

ing: for the dough, plus more as needed
st: Boil the whole potatoes in salted water for 20 minutes until a knife slides in easily. Drain, cool, peel and roughly mash.
Mix the semolina, flour, baking soda and a pinch of salt. Add [[0.33 cup]] water a little at a time and knead for 5 minutes to a stiff dough. Cover with a damp cloth and rest for 20 minutes.
Make the tamarind water by stirring the tamarind paste, [[1 cup]] cold water, sugar, cumin and black salt together until smooth. Chill it.
Mix the mashed potatoes with the chickpeas, onion, chilies, cilantro and salt for the filling.
Roll the dough out very thin and cut small rounds with a small cup or cutter. Keep the cut rounds covered so they do not dry out.
Heat the oil to 350°F (175°C). Fry the rounds a few at a time, pressing them gently under the oil with a spoon so they puff, for about 1 minute until golden.
Drain on paper towels and cool completely so the puris turn crisp.
Tap a hole in the top of each puri, spoon in the filling, pour in a little tamarind water and eat immediately.
Rinse the lentils in a few changes of water until the water runs mostly clear.
Put the lentils in a pot with [[4 cups]] water, the turmeric, half of the onion and the slit chilies. Bring to a boil and skim off any foam.
Reduce the heat, partly cover, and simmer for 20 minutes until the lentils are completely soft.
Whisk or mash the dal until smooth and soupy. Add salt and a splash of hot water if it is too thick.
Heat the oil in a small pan over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 20 seconds.
Add the garlic and remaining onion and fry for 4 to 5 minutes until golden brown.
Pour the sizzling mixture into the dal, stir once, and cover for 2 minutes so the flavors blend.
Top with cilantro and serve with rice.
Put the whole potatoes in a pot, cover with salted water and bring to a boil.
Cook for 20 to 25 minutes until a knife slides in easily.
Drain the potatoes and let them cool until you can handle them, then peel.
Mash the potatoes in a bowl with a fork, leaving a few small lumps.
Add the onion, chilies, cilantro and salt.
Drizzle with the mustard oil and mix well with your hands or a spoon. Taste and add more salt or chili if you like.
Serve at room temperature with rice and dal.
Toss the shrimp with [[0.5 tsp]] turmeric and salt and leave for 10 minutes.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Sear the shrimp for 1 minute per side until just pink, then remove them to a plate.
Lower the heat and melt the ghee in the same pan. Add the cinnamon, cardamom, cloves and bay leaves and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the grated onion and cook for 8 minutes, stirring, until soft and pale gold with no dark color.
Stir in the ginger and [[0.5 tsp]] turmeric and cook for 1 minute.
Pour in the coconut milk and [[0.5 cup]] water, add the sugar and salt, and simmer gently for 10 minutes until slightly thickened.
Add the shrimp and slit chilies and cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the shrimp are opaque and curled.
Stir in the garam masala, remove from the heat, and serve with steamed rice.
Mix the coconut and jaggery in a small pan with the cardamom. Cook over low heat for 5 minutes, stirring, until sticky and well combined. Cool completely.
Bring [[1 cup]] water, the milk and the salt to a boil in a pot.
Put the rice flour in a large bowl and pour in the hot liquid, stirring with a spoon until a rough dough forms. Cover for 10 minutes.
When cool enough to touch, knead the dough for 3 minutes until smooth and soft.
Divide the dough into 12 balls. Flatten each into a thin round, about the size of your palm.
Place a spoonful of filling in the middle, fold the dough over to a half-moon and press the edges to seal.
Line a steamer basket with parchment or a clean damp cloth. Arrange the pitha without touching.
Steam over boiling water for 12 to 15 minutes until the dough is shiny and firm.
Serve the pitha warm, straight from the steamer.
Bring the milk to a boil in a large heavy pot, stirring so it does not scorch.
Turn off the heat and stir in the lemon juice a little at a time until the milk separates into curds and clear greenish whey.
Pour into a colander lined with cheesecloth. Rinse under cold water for 1 minute to remove the lemon taste.
Gather the cloth and hang or squeeze it over the sink. Let the curds drain for 30 minutes until crumbly but not dry.
Knead the curds on a clean counter with the heel of your hand for 8 to 10 minutes until completely smooth and slightly greasy. Roll into 12 smooth balls with no cracks.
In a wide pot, boil the sugar, [[5 cups]] water and cardamom until the sugar dissolves.
Drop in the balls, cover, and boil on medium-high for 15 minutes. They will puff to about double in size.
Turn off the heat and add the rose water if using. Let the roshogolla cool in the syrup, then chill before serving.

ing: with live cultures, at room temperature
st: Simmer the milk in a heavy pot over medium-low heat for 30 to 40 minutes, stirring often and scraping the sides, until reduced to about [[3.5 cups]].
In a small pan, heat the sugar with [[2 tbsp]] water over medium heat without stirring until it becomes a deep amber caramel.
Carefully pour the hot milk into the caramel in a slow stream. It will sputter and the caramel will harden, so keep stirring until it dissolves.
Add the jaggery and stir until dissolved. Remove from the heat.
Cool the milk until it is lukewarm, about 110°F (43°C), warm to the touch but comfortable.
Whisk the yogurt in a bowl with a ladle of the warm milk, then stir it into the pot.
Pour into a clay pot or small jars and cover tightly.
Leave in a warm, draft-free place such as the oven with only the light on, for 8 to 10 hours until set.
Chill for at least 2 hours before serving.
Toast the cumin seeds in a dry pan over medium heat for 1 minute until fragrant.
Grind the toasted cumin to a fine powder with a mortar or spice grinder.
Blend the mint, cilantro, green chili and [[0.5 cup]] of the cold water until smooth.
Add the yogurt, the rest of the water, the ground cumin, black salt, pepper and sugar. Blend again until frothy.
Taste and adjust the salt and chili.
Chill in the fridge for 30 minutes so the flavors blend.
Pour over ice and serve cold with biryani or rich meat dishes.
Rub [[0.33 cup]] ghee into the flour, sugar and salt with your fingertips until it looks like damp sand and holds when pinched.
Add the warm milk and just enough water to bring a stiff dough together. Knead 5 minutes, then rest covered for 30 minutes.
Divide into 8 balls. Roll each into a thin round, spread with a little ghee, fold into a half-moon and then into a triangle.
Roll the triangle out again into a round about 5 inches wide and sprinkle with sesame seeds, pressing them in lightly.
Preheat the oven to 400°F and arrange the rounds on a lined baking tray.
Bake 15 minutes until deep golden and crisp, flipping once halfway. Cool on a rack so they crisp more.
nt: Best swap: use unsalted butter in place of ghee in a 1:1 ratio, but bake 2 minutes less as it browns faster.

st: Toast the puffed rice in a dry pan over low heat for 2 minutes until it feels crisp again. Pour it into a large mixing bowl.
Add the onion, tomato, potato, green chili and peanuts to the rice.
Drizzle in the mustard oil, add the chaat masala and a pinch of salt, then toss gently with a lifting motion so the rice does not break.
Squeeze in the lime juice and add the cilantro, tossing once more.
Taste and add more salt, chili or lime. Serve right away in paper cones, because the rice goes soft within 10 minutes.
nt: No cook, just toss (rice toasted in a dry pan)
Best swap: if mustard oil is hard to find, use 1 tbsp olive oil plus 0.25 tsp wasabi paste or yellow mustard for a similar bite.
